answer:
**An agent needs both a desk and a notebook, plus a way to find the actual code.** Working memory is the small current context: goal, constraints, active files, latest failure, and next step. Episodic memory records what was tried and why it failed. A repository index answers where relevant definitions and callers live. These serve different retrieval needs. [1](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents)

Consider a failing authentication test. Working memory holds the exact assertion and affected endpoint. An episode records that changing cookie lifetime did not fix the failure because the cookie was never attached. An AST or symbol index locates the middleware and its callers. The agent should then read the current source, not edit from an old summary.

Large command outputs belong in artifacts with paths and short summaries. Keep the decisive error lines in context and retrieve more when necessary. Record repository revision, file paths, and provenance with persistent memories; otherwise a useful observation from yesterday can become a misleading fact after a refactor.

Checkpoint the remaining task, verified changes, unresolved hypotheses, and tests already run before context is compressed. Memory should help avoid repeated failed work without turning old hypotheses into unquestionable truth. The completion criterion is an inspected change with relevant validation. A long history of tool calls is not itself evidence that the bug was fixed.

**Technical details and references.**

Keep a compact working state containing the goal, constraints, current hypothesis, relevant file locations, and recent bounded command output. Store episodic records of attempted fixes, observed failures, and why approaches were rejected. Maintain a version-aware semantic/lexical/AST index for finding code, but retrieve exact current files before editing. [1](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)

Every memory entry should record provenance and repository revision; stale summaries must not override current code or user instructions. Save large logs as artifacts and retrieve targeted sections instead of repeatedly inserting them into context. Checkpoints should include remaining work and validation results.

Separate planning from tool authorization, run code in an isolated environment, and require tests or inspection to verify completion. More memory is useful only when relevant, current, and distinguishable from untrusted repository content.
